parts:
Hello,

Another question regarding cluster size and populations that are not arranged in groups but just ocassionally.
I study deer density in dry forest and we often see them in groups of 2-4 inviduals buy mainly 1 individual. We have been analysing them as clusters since 2005 and we just recently realise distance terminology assumes clusters are herds, schools, pride, etc. So we decided to ungroup individuals and treat them as separate sightings. We realise that by doing this it could affect the model as it is easier to spot them when they are in groups but as I said they are more often found by themselves. Is there a correction for this events when there is more than one? how should we treat these events?

thank you again ,

Laura

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] cluster size / individuals in small groups
parts:
Laura:

You are correct that detectability of animals may be enhanced when clusters are large.  That can be incorporated into analyses by treating cluster size as a covariate influencing the detection function.  However, it is fine to "ungroup" sightings as you say, and treat detections as multiple detections at the same perpendicular distance.  The consequence of this "ungrouping" was investigated via simulation by Buckland et al. (2010) in a paper entitled  
Design and Analysis of Line Transect Surveys for Primates
published in International Journal of Primatology .  
http://doi:10.1007/s10764-010-9431-5

Those consequences were found to be small (bias<0.13) when simulating groups of size 3-30.

Cluster size/ungrouped data

I have read that loose population patterns such as the deer population in my study area are more difficult to model, I am not sure why is this. For example I have average cluster size is 1.46 and correlation  0.0499. I decided to try running analysis using cluster size and the ungrouped data.  When I run with cluster size it ran ok but a soon as I marked the density output option a warning message appeared** Warning: Size bias adjustment has increased expected cluster size. **

When I ran ungrouped data with it came green light without truncation then 150m came ok as well and when I tried with 100m it came a warning light ** Warning: Parameters are being constrained to obtain monotonicity. ** When I ran with 50m it came out green again, this is the smallest AIC I´ve got 1937.33

Loose animal aggregations make estimating group size difficult.  The expected pattern of data collected in the field is that small groups of animals are likely to be undetected at large distances; consequently the average size of detected groups *overestimates* the average group size in the population (the size bias problem).  Distance attempts to correct for size bias using regression; in your case Distance has alerted you to the fact that for your data, the regression adjustment has increased rather than decreased expected group size in the population.

Binning (or grouping) your distances need only be performed when the recorded exact distances are suspect (perhaps see below).  The monotonicity message is simply a report that Distance has fitted a model where detection probability continues to decrease as perpendicular distance increases; although your data show a pattern wherein there are elevated numbers of detections at some large distances.  Not an error, simply a report.

severe ‘spike’ at 0 distance

This is an unpleasant situation that you have inherited from the preceding 10 years of data collection.  Your diagnosis of the problem (observers rounding detections to zero because it was near the trail) is a common difficulty.  If the spike is real, i.e. detectability really does fall rapidly at short distances from the transect, then you need a model that attempts to fit the spike.  On the other hand, if the spike is artificial and caused by rounding, then a model that does not try to fit the spike (such as a half-normal) is the better option (but will fit the observed data poorly).  The decision will have to be taken based on opinion rather than data.  Clever analysis is not the remedy to this problem, improved field procedures are the remedy.

I understand from other posts that a p ≤0.05 like the one Ive got in both cases for the KS test tells me so strong eviudence of lack of fit can I suspect this is due to the spike at cero distance? parts:
Laura:

You need to make a judgement about the data you have.  You are trying to fit a model to the *process* that gave rise to the data, rather than fit every bump and valley of your data.  Do not be completely driven by goodness of fit and AIC scores. 

Apply a smooth (continuously decreasing) function to your data.  You may choose to bin the distance out to 9m to account for the rounding problem.  You will present the histograms in your report and describe your understanding of them.  The goodness of fit statistics help you understand your data, but they should not drive incessant tinkering with data to achieve fit.

There are no easy solutions when data have a spike at zero; every remedy you employ will have an element of opinion involved.

You need to make a judgement about the data you have.  You are trying to fit a model to the *process* that gave rise to the data, rather than fit every bump and valley of your data.  Do not be completely driven by goodness of fit and AIC scores. 

Apply a smooth (continuously decreasing) function to your data.  You may choose to bin the distance out to 9m to account for the rounding problem.  You will present the histograms in your report and describe your understanding of them.  The goodness of fit statistics help you understand your data, but they should not drive incessant tinkering with data to achieve fit.

Loose animal aggregations make estimating group size difficult.  The expected pattern of data collected in the field is that small groups of animals are likely to be undetected at large distances; consequently the average size of detected groups *overestimates* the average group size in the population (the size bias problem).  Distance attempts to correct for size bias using regression; in your case Distance has alerted you to the fact that for your data, the regression adjustment has increased rather than decreased expected group size in the population.

Binning (or grouping) your distances need only be performed when the recorded exact distances are suspect (perhaps see below).  The monotonicity message is simply a report that Distance has fitted a model where detection probability continues to decrease as perpendicular distance increases; although your data show a pattern wherein there are elevated numbers of detections at some large distances.  Not an error, simply a report.

This is an unpleasant situation that you have inherited from the preceding 10 years of data collection.  Your diagnosis of the problem (observers rounding detections to zero because it was near the trail) is a common difficulty.  If the spike is real, i.e. detectability really does fall rapidly at short distances from the transect, then you need a model that attempts to fit the spike.  On the other hand, if the spike is artificial and caused by rounding, then a model that does not try to fit the spike (such as a half-normal) is the better option (but will fit the observed data poorly).  The decision will have to be taken based on opinion rather than data.  Clever analysis is not the remedy to this problem, improved field procedures are the remedy.
